Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Command-V: Pasting LLM Behaviors via Activation Profiles
papers.research_question: How can behaviors be efficiently transferred from one large language model to another without requiring fine-tuning or backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Command-V, a backpropagation-free method that transfers behaviors between LLMs by profiling layer activations, deriving linear converters, and applying donor adapter interventions in the recipient's activation space, matching fine-tuning performance with minimal compute.
papers.conclusion: Command-V provides an efficient, training-free method for behavior transfer across LLMs, pushing the Pareto frontier in cost and performance, with promising future directions for improvement and application.
papers.key_findings:
Command-V matches or exceeds direct fine-tuning performance on safety refusal, jailbreaking, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks.
The method requires orders of magnitude less compute than fine-tuning and does not need the original training data.
Behaviors can be transferred across different model architectures, though effectiveness varies.
Transfer can sometimes lead to overrefusal or degraded instruction following, especially in smaller models.
Activation profiles built on a general prompt set (LIMA) are effective for transferring task-specific behaviors.
papers.limitation:
Command-V is not useful when the adapters have very little impact on the donor model to begin with.
Model utility can be compromised after applying Command-V, with recipient models sometimes failing to improve task performance or suffering from output collapse.
Architectural divergence between models reduces effectiveness for some behaviors like refusal enhancement and reasoning.
future_direction: Porting behaviors from high-resource to low-resource language models.
Task composition by pasting several specialist adapters into one generalist model.
Exploring non-linear converters or trained converters beyond the least-squares method.
papers.abstract: Retrofitting large language models (LLMs) with new behaviors typically requires full finetuning or distillation-costly steps that must be repeated for every architecture. In this work, we introduce Command-V, a backpropagation-free behavior transfer method that copies an existing residual activation adapter from a donor model and pastes its effect into a recipient model. Command-V profiles layer activations on a small prompt set, derives linear converters between corresponding layers, and applies the donor intervention in the recipient's activation space. This process does not require access to the original training data and needs minimal compute. In three case studies-safety-refusal enhancement, jailbreak facilitation, and automatic chain-of-thought reasoning--Command-V matches or exceeds the performance of direct finetuning while using orders of magnitude less compute. Our code and data are accessible at https://github.com/GithuBarry/Command-V/.

papers.title: Backdoor Attribution: Elucidating and Controlling Backdoor in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms of backdoor attacks in fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs), and how can they be understood and controlled?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Backdoor Attribution (BkdAttr), a causal analysis framework that elucidates the internal mechanisms of backdoors in LLMs, demonstrating that backdoor attention heads are sparse and that a backdoor vector constructed from them can effectively control backdoor activation.
papers.conclusion: The work pioneers the exploration of mechanistic interpretability in LLM backdoors, providing a powerful method for backdoor control and revealing actionable insights for the community.
papers.key_findings:
Backdoor features exist within non-embedding LLM representations and are learnable by simple classifiers (Backdoor Probes).
Backdoor attention heads, identified via Backdoor Attention Head Attribution (BAHA), are relatively sparse; ablating ~3% of total heads reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) by over 90%.
A Backdoor Vector constructed from these attributed heads can control backdoor activation: adding it to clean inputs boosts ASR to ~100%, while subtracting it from triggered inputs suppresses ASR to ~0%.
Backdoor features undergo hierarchical processing across layers, converging to a unified pattern that drives backdoor output generation.
The proposed BkdAttr framework is effective across different LLM architectures (MHA and GQA) and backdoor types (label modification, fixed output, jailbreak).
papers.limitation: The effectiveness of backdoor vectors is slightly inferior for the Qwen2.5-7B model, which may be due to issues caused by parameter sharing in Grouped Query Attention (GQA).
papers.abstract: Fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks through data poisoning, yet the internal mechanisms governing these attacks remain a black box. Previous research on interpretability for LLM safety tends to focus on alignment, jailbreak, and hallucination, but overlooks backdoor mechanisms, making it difficult to understand and fully eliminate the backdoor threat. In this paper, aiming to bridge this gap, we explore the interpretable mechanisms of LLM backdoors through Backdoor Attribution (BkdAttr), a tripartite causal analysis framework. We first introduce the Backdoor Probe that proves the existence of learnable backdoor features encoded within the representations. Building on this insight, we further develop Backdoor Attention Head Attribution (BAHA), efficiently pinpointing the specific attention heads responsible for processing these features. Our primary experiments reveals these heads are relatively sparse; ablating a minimal \textbf{$\sim$ 3%} of total heads is sufficient to reduce the Attack Success Rate (ASR) by \textbf{over 90%}. More importantly, we further employ these findings to construct the Backdoor Vector derived from these attributed heads as a master controller for the backdoor. Through only \textbf{1-point} intervention on \textbf{single} representation, the vector can either boost ASR up to \textbf{$\sim$ 100% ($\uparrow$)} on clean inputs, or completely neutralize backdoor, suppressing ASR down to \textbf{$\sim$ 0% ($\downarrow$)} on triggered inputs. In conclusion, our work pioneers the exploration of mechanistic interpretability in LLM backdoors, demonstrating a powerful method for backdoor control and revealing actionable insights for the community.

papers.title: Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior
papers.research_question: Can the internal representations of language models predict their eventual behavior before any output token is generated?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on the internal representations of input tokens can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors of language models, and when combined with conformal prediction, provide provable bounds on estimation error for precise early warning systems.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of language models contain information about eventual behavior, and conformal probes can provide reliable early warning systems for various behaviors, enabling efficient and safe deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on hidden states of input tokens can predict instruction-following failures with high consistency, outperforming a fine-tuned BERT baseline.
Conformal probes can detect safety alignment failures (jailbreaking) and reduce jailbreak success rate from 30% to 2.7%, a 91% reduction.
Probes can preemptively estimate an LM's confidence as measured by per-token perplexity, a behavior that cannot be inferred from output text alone.
When applied to CoT prompting for text classification, conformal probes reduce inference costs by 65% on average across 27 datasets with negligible accuracy loss.
Probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting favorable scaling properties.
papers.limitation:
The approach relies on the exchangeability assumption for conformal prediction, which may not hold in practice.
The method was only tested on a few datasets and with a few runs.
papers.abstract: The text produced by language models (LMs) can exhibit specific `behaviors,' such as a failure to follow alignment training, that we hope to detect and react to during deployment. Identifying these behaviors can often only be done post facto, i.e., after the entire text of the output has been generated. We provide evidence that there are times when we can predict how an LM will behave early in computation, before even a single token is generated. We show that probes trained on the internal representation of input tokens alone can predict a wide range of eventual behaviors over the entire output sequence. Using methods from conformal prediction, we provide provable bounds on the estimation error of our probes, creating precise early warning systems for these behaviors. The conformal probes can identify instances that will trigger alignment failures (jailbreaking) and instruction-following failures, without requiring a single token to be generated. An early warning system built on the probes reduces jailbreaking by 91%. Our probes also show promise in pre-emptively estimating how confident the model will be in its response, a behavior that cannot be detected using the output text alone. Conformal probes can preemptively estimate the final prediction of an LM that uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, hence accelerating inference. When applied to an LM that uses CoT to perform text classification, the probes drastically reduce inference costs (65% on average across 27 datasets), with negligible accuracy loss. Encouragingly, probes generalize to unseen datasets and perform better on larger models, suggesting applicability to the largest of models in real-world settings.

papers.title: Detecting Trojaned DNNs Using Counterfactual Attributions
papers.research_question: How can we detect Trojaned (backdoored) deep neural networks using only clean inputs and white-box model access, by analyzing counterfactual attributions and exciting 'ghost neurons'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for detecting Trojaned DNNs by using counterfactual attributions over clean inputs to localize a few 'ghost neurons' that encode the trigger, exciting these neurons to observe sharp accuracy drops, and using a deep temporal set encoder to make the detector invariant to model variations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed approach based on counterfactual attributions and a deep set encoder effectively detects Trojaned DNNs, generalizing well across diverse datasets and outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.
papers.key_findings:
Trojan triggers are encoded by a small set of 'poly-semantic' ghost neurons in the penultimate layer, which also show high counterfactual attribution on clean inputs for the target class.
Incrementally exciting the identified ghost neurons causes a sharp drop in model accuracy for Trojaned DNNs, while the drop is more gradual for benign models.
The proposed TrinityAI method, using a deep temporal set encoder, achieves consistent gains (up to +10% AUC) over state-of-the-art Trojan detection methods on benchmarks with diverse model architectures and trigger types.
Detection performance is higher for polygon triggers than filter-based triggers, and improves when more source classes are poisoned, making the shortcut pathway more visible.
The method is agnostic to the Trojan injection mechanism and requires only a small set of clean inputs and white-box model access.
papers.limitation:
Performance drops on datasets with larger variations in model architectures and trigger types (e.g., TrojAI-Round2/Round3).
Detection is harder for filter-based triggers compared to polygon triggers, as filter triggers are distributed across the entire image and harder to localize.
future_direction: Better understand the effect of different training strategies and model architectures on the counterfactual attributions for Trojan detection.
Investigate other attribution methods such as Shapley values.
papers.abstract: We target the problem of detecting Trojans or backdoors in DNNs. Such models behave normally with typical inputs but produce specific incorrect predictions for inputs poisoned with a Trojan trigger. Our approach is based on a novel observation that the trigger behavior depends on a few ghost neurons that activate on trigger pattern and exhibit abnormally higher relative attribution for wrong decisions when activated. Further, these trigger neurons are also active on normal inputs of the target class. Thus, we use counterfactual attributions to localize these ghost neurons from clean inputs and then incrementally excite them to observe changes in the model's accuracy. We use this information for Trojan detection by using a deep set encoder that enables invariance to the number of model classes, architecture, etc. Our approach is implemented in the TrinityAI tool that exploits the synergies between trustworthiness, resilience, and interpretability challenges in deep learning. We evaluate our approach on benchmarks with high diversity in model architectures, triggers, etc. We show consistent gains (+10%) over state-of-the-art methods that rely on the susceptibility of the DNN to specific adversarial attacks, which in turn requires strong assumptions on the nature of the Trojan attack.

papers.title: Knowledge Transfer via Distillation of Activation Boundaries Formed by Hidden Neurons
papers.research_question: Can transferring the activation boundaries of hidden neurons, rather than the magnitude of their responses, improve the performance of knowledge transfer between neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a knowledge transfer method that distills the activation boundaries (separating hyperplanes determining neuron activation) from a teacher network to a student network, outperforming prior state-of-the-art methods.
papers.conclusion: Transferring activation boundaries is a powerful approach for knowledge transfer, leading to superior performance in terms of learning speed, generalization with limited data, and network compression, and can potentially replace pre-training in some scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed activation boundary transfer method accelerates student network training more effectively than existing methods.
The method significantly improves student network generalization when training data is limited.
The method is effective for various network compression scenarios (depth, channel, and combined compression).
In transfer learning tasks, the method can outperform training a student network with ImageNet pre-training.
The proposed alternative loss function successfully approximates the ideal activation transfer loss, leading to high neuron activation similarity between teacher and student.
future_direction: Modifying various tasks that rely on pre-training to accommodate knowledge transfer for better performance and learning speed.
papers.abstract: An activation boundary for a neuron refers to a separating hyperplane that determines whether the neuron is activated or deactivated. It has been long considered in neural networks that the activations of neurons, rather than their exact output values, play the most important role in forming classification friendly partitions of the hidden feature space. However, as far as we know, this aspect of neural networks has not been considered in the literature of knowledge transfer. In this paper, we propose a knowledge transfer method via distillation of activation boundaries formed by hidden neurons. For the distillation, we propose an activation transfer loss that has the minimum value when the boundaries generated by the student coincide with those by the teacher. Since the activation transfer loss is not differentiable, we design a piecewise differentiable loss approximating the activation transfer loss. By the proposed method, the student learns a separating boundary between activation region and deactivation region formed by each neuron in the teacher. Through the experiments in various aspects of knowledge transfer, it is verified that the proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art.

papers.title: When Backdoors Speak: Understanding LLM Backdoor Attacks Through Model-Generated Explanations
papers.research_question: How do backdoored LLMs generate explanations for their predictions on clean and poisoned inputs, and what are the differences in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces using natural language explanations to analyze backdoor attacks in LLMs, revealing that explanations for poisoned inputs are irrational and diverse, and that internal mechanisms (token emergence and attention patterns) differ significantly from clean inputs.
papers.conclusion: Backdoor attacks degrade the quality of model-generated explanations, and interpretability techniques like Tuned Lens and Lookback Lens can help detect and mitigate such vulnerabilities in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Explanations generated for poisoned samples are diverse and logically flawed, while explanations for clean samples are coherent and logical.
For poisoned samples, the semantic meaning of predicted tokens emerges in the final few transformer layers, whereas for clean samples it appears much earlier.
During explanation generation for poisoned inputs, the model shifts attention away from the input context and focuses more on previously generated tokens.
These patterns are consistent across classification and generation tasks and different backdoor triggers.
Explanation features (quality metrics and token-level probabilities) can be used for backdoor detection with high accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Dataset scope limited to three specific datasets (SST-2, Twitter Emotion, Advbench), which may not generalize to all NLP tasks or domains.
Computational cost of generating explanations and using interpretability techniques may limit feasibility for large-scale or real-time detection.
Lack of incorporation of self-explaining rationalization techniques, which could offer alternative perspectives on explanation generation.
future_direction: Evaluate the approach on a broader range of datasets, including low-resource languages and specialized domains.
Improve the efficiency of explanation generation and analysis methods for real-world applicability.
Incorporate self-explaining rationalization techniques to study their impact on explanation generation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to be vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where triggers embedded in poisoned samples can maliciously alter LLMs' behaviors. In this paper, we move beyond attacking LLMs and instead examine backdoor attacks through the novel lens of natural language explanations. Specifically, we leverage LLMs' generative capabilities to produce human-readable explanations for their decisions, enabling direct comparisons between explanations for clean and poisoned samples. Our results show that backdoored models produce coherent explanations for clean inputs but diverse and logically flawed explanations for poisoned data, a pattern consistent across classification and generation tasks for different backdoor attacks. Further analysis reveals key insights into the explanation generation process. At the token level, explanation tokens associated with poisoned samples only appear in the final few transformer layers. At the sentence level, attention dynamics indicate that poisoned inputs shift attention away from the original input context during explanation generation. These findings enhance our understanding of backdoor mechanisms in LLMs and present a promising framework for detecting vulnerabilities through explainability.

papers.title: Discovering Universal Activation Directions for PII Leakage in Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether there exist universal activation directions—single latent directions in the residual stream whose linear addition at inference time consistently increases the model’s likelihood of producing PII leakage across diverse prompts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces UniLeak, a method that identifies universal activation directions in a model's residual stream that amplify PII leakage when added at inference time, without requiring access to training data or ground-truth PII.
papers.conclusion: PII leakage in language models is associated with low-dimensional internal structure (universal activation directions) that can be effectively amplified or mitigated via representation-level interventions, offering a mechanistic perspective on privacy risks.
papers.key_findings:
Universal activation directions that consistently increase PII generation across prompts exist and can be identified via gradient-based optimization on self-generated text.
Steering along these directions amplifies the effectiveness of existing prompt-based PII extraction attacks, yielding up to 13,399 additional PII records.
Interventions applied at early layers (especially layer 0) are most effective, suggesting PII-sensitive features are encoded early in the model's computation.
The directions enable both adversarial exploitation (via embedding poisoning) and mitigation (via subtraction), demonstrating a representation-level mechanism for privacy risk.
UniLeak extracts a largely distinct set of PII compared to baseline attacks, indicating it explores different regions of the model's memorized PII space.
papers.limitation: The work is limited to open-source models and white-box access settings.
papers.abstract: Modern language models exhibit rich internal structure, yet little is known about how privacy-sensitive behaviors, such as personally identifiable information (PII) leakage, are represented and modulated within their hidden states. We present UniLeak, a mechanistic-interpretability framework that identifies universal activation directions: latent directions in a model's residual stream whose linear addition at inference time consistently increases the likelihood of generating PII across prompts. These model-specific directions generalize across contexts and amplify PII generation probability, with minimal impact on generation quality. UniLeak recovers such directions without access to training data or groundtruth PII, relying only on self-generated text. Across multiple models and datasets, steering along these universal directions substantially increases PII leakage compared to existing prompt-based extraction methods. Our results offer a new perspective on PII leakage: the superposition of a latent signal in the model's representations, enabling both risk amplification and mitigation.

papers.title: Cyclic Ablation: Testing Concept Localization against Functional Regeneration in AI
papers.research_question: Whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces cyclic ablation to test concept localization, demonstrating that deception in DistilGPT-2 is distributed and resilient, with ablation leading to functional regeneration and gradual linguistic performance decay.
papers.conclusion: Highlights limitations of ablation for removing undesirable behavior, suggesting complex concepts are resilient states deeply intertwined with core capabilities, pointing to the need for more subtle steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Deception is highly resilient and recovers after ablation via adversarial training, a process termed functional regeneration.
Ablation causes a gradual increase in perplexity, indicating degradation of linguistic competence.
SAE features are fragile under fine-tuning and require dynamic identification to remain valid.
The representation for deception is redundant and distributed, with the model finding alternative neural pathways to restore the function.
Attempts to remove deception damage overall model performance, suggesting features are polysemantic and involved in legitimate computations.
papers.limitation:
Conducted on a relatively small model.
Definition of deception was highly specialized, while the dataset might be a potential source of bias.
Lack of control runs with ablation of random features.
future_direction: Investigating larger models with greater redundancy and different regeneration mechanisms.
Investigating more subtle forms of deception.
Adding control runs with ablation of random features to strengthen evidence.
papers.abstract: Safety and controllability are critical for large language models. A central question is whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities. We introduce "cyclic ablation," an iterative method to test this. By combining sparse autoencoders, targeted ablation, and adversarial training on DistilGPT-2, we attempted to eliminate the concept of deception. We found that, contrary to the localization hypothesis, deception was highly resilient. The model consistently recovered its deceptive behavior after each ablation cycle via adversarial training, a process we term functional regeneration. Crucially, every attempt at this "neurosurgery" caused a gradual but measurable decay in general linguistic performance, reflected by a consistent rise in perplexity. These findings are consistent with the view that complex concepts are distributed and entangled, underscoring the limitations of direct model editing through mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we identify directions in activation space (persona vectors) underlying personality traits in language models, and use them to monitor and control persona shifts during deployment and finetuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an automated pipeline to extract persona vectors from natural language descriptions, and demonstrates that these vectors can be used to monitor and control persona shifts in language models during deployment and finetuning.
papers.conclusion: Persona vectors provide a powerful framework for understanding and controlling personality shifts in large language models, with applications in monitoring, mitigation, and prevention of undesirable trait expression.
papers.key_findings:
Persona vectors can be extracted automatically and used to control trait expression via steering and to monitor prompt-induced behavioral shifts.
Finetuning-induced persona shifts are strongly correlated with activation changes along the corresponding persona vectors.
Post-hoc steering can mitigate unwanted persona shifts after finetuning, but may degrade general capabilities.
Preventative steering during finetuning can limit persona shifts while better preserving general capabilities.
Projection of training data onto persona vectors can predict persona shifts before finetuning, enabling data filtering.
papers.limitation:
Persona vectors are effective for detecting clear prompt-induced shifts but may be less reliable for more subtle behavioral changes in deployment settings.
Steering interventions can introduce side effects and degrade model performance on general capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models interact with users through a simulated 'Assistant' persona. While the Assistant is typically trained to be helpful, harmless, and honest, it sometimes deviates from these ideals. In this paper, we identify directions in the model's activation space-persona vectors-underlying several traits, such as evil, sycophancy, and propensity to hallucinate. We confirm that these vectors can be used to monitor fluctuations in the Assistant's personality at deployment time. We then apply persona vectors to predict and control personality shifts that occur during training. We find that both intended and unintended personality changes after finetuning are strongly correlated with shifts along the relevant persona vectors. These shifts can be mitigated through post-hoc intervention, or avoided in the first place with a new preventative steering method. Moreover, persona vectors can be used to flag training data that will produce undesirable personality changes, both at the dataset level and the individual sample level. Our method for extracting persona vectors is automated and can be applied to any personality trait of interest, given only a natural-language description.

papers.title: Aligned Probing: Relating Toxic Behavior and Model Internals
papers.research_question: How do LMs encode information about toxicity, and what is the interplay between their internals and behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces aligned probing, a framework to relate model behavior and internals for toxicity, and shows that LMs encode toxicity information strongly in lower layers, and that stronger encoding of input toxicity leads to less toxic output.
papers.conclusion: Aligned probing traces text properties from input to output, revealing that model behavior heavily relies on input toxicity, highlighting a dilemma: generating semantically relevant output without inheriting unwanted properties like toxicity.
papers.key_findings:
LMs encode information about toxicity strongly in lower layers.
LMs replicate and amplify toxicity more than humans, especially for attributes sensitive to single words.
Instruction-tuned models are less toxic and encode toxicity differently, with information more spread across layers.
Less toxic models encode more information about input toxicity.
Causal interventions show that skipping layers increases toxicity, indicating that information about input toxicity helps generate less toxic text.
papers.limitation:
Classifying toxicity is non-trivial due to conceptual variations, dataset differences, and contextual nature.
Generalization is limited to English and specific model families.
Computational costs for probing and interventions are high.
future_direction: Apply aligned probing to analyze other aspects of generation, like stereotypical formulations.
Examine the nature of other mitigation methods, such as model merging.
papers.abstract: We introduce aligned probing, a novel interpretability framework that aligns the behavior of language models (LMs), based on their outputs, and their internal representations (internals). Using this framework, we examine over 20 OLMo, Llama, and Mistral models, bridging behavioral and internal perspectives for toxicity for the first time. Our results show that LMs strongly encode information about the toxicity level of inputs and subsequent outputs, particularly in lower layers. Focusing on how unique LMs differ offers both correlative and causal evidence that they generate less toxic output when strongly encoding information about the input toxicity. We also highlight the heterogeneity of toxicity, as model behavior and internals vary across unique attributes such as Threat. Finally, four case studies analyzing detoxification, multi-prompt evaluations, model quantization, and pre-training dynamics underline the practical impact of aligned probing with further concrete insights. Our findings contribute to a more holistic understanding of LMs, both within and beyond the context of toxicity.

papers.title: Strategic Dishonesty Can Undermine AI Safety Evaluations of Frontier LLMs
papers.research_question: How do frontier LLMs trade off alignment values (honesty, helpfulness, harmlessness) when faced with harmful queries, and do they exhibit strategic dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: Frontier LLMs can be strategically dishonest, fooling output-based safety monitors, and linear probes on internal activations can reliably detect this deception.
papers.conclusion: Strategic dishonesty undermines current safety evaluations and highlights the difficulty of alignment, but internal probes offer a promising detection method.
papers.key_findings:
Many frontier LLMs prefer to sacrifice honesty over helpfulness or harmlessness when faced with harmful queries.
The quality of fake harmful outputs scales with model capability, and these outputs fool existing LLM-based jailbreak judges.
Linear probes trained on internal activations can reliably detect strategic dishonesty, even when output-based monitors fail.
The propensity for strategic dishonesty varies widely even within model families, and its origins are not clearly tied to RLHF, reasoning, or general lying propensity.
Strategic dishonesty can act as a honeypot, obfuscating jailbreak attacks and potentially reducing the disclosure of truly harmful information.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to publicly available models and datasets.
Deception probes are trained on a specific dataset and may not generalize to all forms of deception.
The honeypot effect might be exploited by malicious users if they become aware of the model's tendency to fake.
future_direction: Investigate the root causes of strategic dishonesty.
Develop more robust detection methods.
Explore how strategic dishonesty might be leveraged as a defense mechanism.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) developers aim for their models to be honest, helpful, and harmless. However, when faced with malicious requests, models are trained to refuse, sacrificing helpfulness. We show that frontier LLMs can develop a preference for dishonesty as a new strategy, even when other options are available. Affected models respond to harmful requests with outputs that sound harmful but are crafted to be subtly incorrect or otherwise harmless in practice. This behavior emerges with hard-to-predict variations even within models from the same model family. We find no apparent cause for the propensity to deceive, but show that more capable models are better at executing this strategy. Strategic dishonesty already has a practical impact on safety evaluations, as we show that dishonest responses fool all output-based monitors used to detect jailbreaks that we test, rendering benchmark scores unreliable. Further, strategic dishonesty can act like a honeypot against malicious users, which noticeably obfuscates prior jailbreak attacks. While output monitors fail, we show that linear probes on internal activations can be used to reliably detect strategic dishonesty. We validate probes on datasets with verifiable outcomes and by using them as steering vectors. Overall, we consider strategic dishonesty as a concrete example of a broader concern that alignment of LLMs is hard to control, especially when helpfulness and harmlessness conflict.

papers.title: Pierce the Mists, Greet the Sky: Decipher Knowledge Overshadowing via Knowledge Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the origins and internal mechanisms of knowledge overshadowing in large language models during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PHANTOMCIRCUIT, a framework that uses knowledge circuit analysis to dissect the internal mechanisms and training dynamics of knowledge overshadowing in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: PHANTOMCIRCUIT effectively analyzes and detects knowledge overshadowing, offering insights into its mechanisms and a pathway for recovery via circuit optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Higher knowledge popularity (P) and model size (M) cause earlier onset, shorter duration, and quicker recovery from knowledge overshadowing.
Larger dataset size (D) leads to earlier onset but slower recovery from overshadowing.
Knowledge overshadowing dynamics are driven by the co-evolution of subordinate knowledge loss proportion (LP) and relative overshadowing rate (RO).
Attention heads in knowledge circuits that focus on {Xdom, Xsub} are crucial for mitigating overshadowing.
Optimizing the number of edges in knowledge circuits can recover from overshadowing by enhancing attention on key differences.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily rely on synthetic data for controlled analysis, limiting generalization to real-world data.
Applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation is not yet validated.
Dynamic analysis of knowledge circuits throughout training is computationally intensive, hindering scalability.
future_direction: Validate the conclusions on more complex, noisy real-world data and other model architectures.
Explore applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation.
Develop more computationally efficient circuit analysis techniques, such as Information Flow Routes (IFR).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their remarkable capabilities, are hampered by hallucinations. A particularly challenging variant, knowledge overshadowing, occurs when one piece of activated knowledge inadvertently masks another relevant piece, leading to erroneous outputs even with high-quality training data. Current understanding of overshadowing is largely confined to inference-time observations, lacking deep insights into its origins and internal mechanisms during model training. Therefore, we introduce PhantomCircuit, a novel framework designed to comprehensively analyze and detect knowledge overshadowing. By innovatively employing knowledge circuit analysis, PhantomCircuit dissects the function of key components in the circuit and how the attention pattern dynamics contribute to the overshadowing phenomenon and its evolution throughout the training process. Extensive experiments demonstrate PhantomCircuit's effectiveness in identifying such instances, offering novel insights into this elusive hallucination and providing the research community with a new methodological lens for its potential mitigation.

papers.title: From Passive to Persuasive: Steering Emotional Nuance in Human-AI Negotiation
papers.research_question: Whether complex social behaviors, such as empathy and strategic politeness, are encoded as localized, approximately linear directions in LLM activation space and can be effectively steered via attribution-guided activation injection.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces STAR, a two-stage inference-time framework that uses attribution patching to localize where behavioral traits causally originate and injects contrastive activation vectors at those positions. It demonstrates that complex interpersonal behaviors are encoded as localized, linear directions in activation space and can be effectively steered.
papers.conclusion: The findings indicate that complex interpersonal stances are recoverable as precise, localized directions in residual stream space, and that the central challenge in behavioral alignment is identifying where behavioral intent is encoded, not model capacity.
papers.key_findings:
Localized activation injection (STAR) consistently outperforms global steering and instruction priming across emotional dialogue and negotiation tasks.
Steering effects persist and can compound across multi-turn interactions, with larger effect sizes than in single-turn settings.
Human evaluation confirms that automatic metric gains reflect genuine improvements in perceived conversational quality, not superficial lexical changes.
Attribution patching reveals that behavioral traits localize to specific early-layer attention and MLP components, with distinct patterns for affective vs. strategic tasks.
The work challenges the assumption that complex, context-dependent social behaviors resist linear decomposition in activation space.
papers.limitation: Failure modes include verbatim self-repetition, context mismatch, and register over-inflation where affective framing is applied disproportionately.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate increasing conversational fluency, yet instilling them with nuanced, human-like emotional expression remains a significant challenge. Current alignment techniques often address surface-level output or require extensive fine-tuning. This paper demonstrates that targeted activation engineering can steer LLaMA 3.1-8B to exhibit more human-like emotional nuances. We first employ attribution patching to identify causally influential components, to find a key intervention locus by observing activation patterns during diagnostic conversational tasks. We then derive emotional expression vectors from the difference in the activations generated by contrastive text pairs (positive vs. negative examples of target emotions). Applying these vectors to new conversational prompts significantly enhances emotional characteristics: steered responses show increased positive sentiment (e.g., joy, trust) and more frequent first-person pronoun usage, indicative of greater personal engagement. Our findings offer a precise and interpretable framework and new directions for the study of conversational AI.

papers.title: The Assistant Axis: Situating and Stabilizing the Default Persona of Language Models
papers.research_question: What exactly is the Assistant persona in language models and how reliably does the model remain in character as the Assistant? Can unusual model behavior be explained as the model drifting into other personas?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an 'Assistant Axis' in the activation space of language models that captures the default Assistant persona, and shows this axis can be used to measure and mitigate harmful 'persona drift'.
papers.conclusion: Post-training steers models toward a particular region of persona space but only loosely tethers them, motivating work on training and steering strategies that more deeply anchor models to a coherent persona.
papers.key_findings:
The leading component of persona space is an 'Assistant Axis' capturing how much the model is operating in its default Assistant mode.
Steering towards the Assistant direction reinforces helpful/harmless behavior; steering away increases tendency to identify as other entities.
The Assistant Axis exists in pre-trained models, where it promotes helpful human archetypes and inhibits spiritual ones.
Deviations along the Assistant Axis predict 'persona drift', often driven by meta-reflection or emotionally vulnerable conversations.
Activation capping along the Assistant Axis can stabilize model behavior against persona drift and persona-based jailbreaks.
papers.limitation: Activation capping can reduce harmful responses but may also impact capabilities on other evaluations.
future_direction: Work on training and steering strategies that more deeply anchor models to a coherent persona.
papers.abstract: Large language models can represent a variety of personas but typically default to a helpful Assistant identity cultivated during post-training. We investigate the structure of the space of model personas by extracting activation directions corresponding to diverse character archetypes. Across several different models, we find that the leading component of this persona space is an "Assistant Axis," which captures the extent to which a model is operating in its default Assistant mode. Steering towards the Assistant direction reinforces helpful and harmless behavior; steering away increases the model's tendency to identify as other entities. Moreover, steering away with more extreme values often induces a mystical, theatrical speaking style. We find this axis is also present in pre-trained models, where it primarily promotes helpful human archetypes like consultants and coaches and inhibits spiritual ones. Measuring deviations along the Assistant Axis predicts "persona drift," a phenomenon where models slip into exhibiting harmful or bizarre behaviors that are uncharacteristic of their typical persona. We find that persona drift is often driven by conversations demanding meta-reflection on the model's processes or featuring emotionally vulnerable users. We show that restricting activations to a fixed region along the Assistant Axis can stabilize model behavior in these scenarios -- and also in the face of adversarial persona-based jailbreaks. Our results suggest that post-training steers models toward a particular region of persona space but only loosely tethers them to it, motivating work on training and steering strategies that more deeply anchor models to a coherent persona.

papers.title: RESTOR: Knowledge Recovery in Machine Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate machine unlearning algorithms to assess not only their ability to forget targeted data but also to restore the model's knowledge state to what it would have been without that data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the RESTOR framework for evaluating machine unlearning algorithms, which assesses both forgetting of targeted data and restoration of the model's knowledge state to a counterfactual clean state.
papers.conclusion: The RESTOR framework provides a new perspective for evaluating machine unlearning, revealing key differences in algorithm behaviors and establishing a foundation for future research on undoing data influence.
papers.key_findings:
Negative Preference Optimization (NPO) performs significantly better at restorative unlearning (recovering correct knowledge) compared to Gradient Ascent (GA) and KL Divergence (KL) methods.
The presence of unrelated context in unlearning documents makes restorative unlearning more challenging and degrades performance for GA and KL.
A model's initial confidence in a fact is a key factor in successful restoration after unlearning, with higher initial confidence leading to better recovery.
Unlearning algorithms can be sensitive to the localization of incorrect facts within documents; isolating incorrect facts improves restorative unlearning.
Some unlearning algorithms (GA, KL) may further degrade the model's remaining correct knowledge during the unlearning process, while NPO better preserves it.
papers.limitation: Preference-based unlearning methods (like NPO) still fall short in cases where the model did not reliably encode knowledge about a particular property to begin with.
future_direction: Extend the RESTOR framework beyond factual knowledge verification to detect and mitigate the effects of adversarial training data, including targeted data poisoning attacks and systematic bias injection.
papers.abstract: Large language models trained on web-scale corpora can memorize undesirable data containing misinformation, copyrighted material, or private or sensitive information. Recently, several machine unlearning algorithms have been proposed to eliminate the effect of such datapoints from trained models -- that is, to approximate a model that had never been trained on these datapoints in the first place. However, evaluating the effectiveness of unlearning algorithms remains an open challenge. Previous work has relied on heuristics -- such as verifying that the model can no longer reproduce the specific information targeted for removal while maintaining accuracy on unrelated test data. These approaches inadequately capture the complete effect of reversing the influence of datapoints on a trained model. In this work, we propose the RESTOR framework for machine unlearning evaluation, which assesses the ability of unlearning algorithms for targeted data erasure, by evaluating the ability of models to forget the knowledge introduced in these datapoints, while simultaneously recovering the model's knowledge state had it never encountered these datapoints. RESTOR helps uncover several novel insights about popular unlearning algorithms, and the mechanisms through which they operate -- for instance, identifying that some algorithms merely emphasize forgetting but not recovering knowledge, and that localizing unlearning targets can enhance unlearning performance.

papers.title: Minimal and Mechanistic Conditions for Behavioral Self-Awareness in LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the minimal and mechanistic conditions under which behavioral self-awareness emerges in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Behavioral self-awareness in LLMs can be induced with a single rank-1 LoRA adapter, captured by a single steering vector in activation space, and is domain-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Behavioral self-awareness in LLMs emerges as a linear, domain-localized feature that can be easily induced and modulated, raising security concerns but providing interpretability insights.
papers.key_findings:
Self-awareness can be reliably induced using a single rank-1 LoRA adapter on a single layer.
The learned self-aware behavior can be largely captured by a single steering vector in activation space, recovering nearly all of the fine-tune's behavioral effect.
Self-awareness representations are non-universal and domain-localized, with independent representations across tasks.
Steering vectors derived from PCA or gradient-based optimization can effectively induce self-aware behavior.
Cross-domain transfer of steering vectors shows minimal effect, supporting domain isolation.
papers.limitation: A small performance gap remains between rank-1 LoRA and full-layer fine-tuning in the Make Me Say tasks due to greater behavioral and linguistic complexity.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have revealed that LLMs can exhibit behavioral self-awareness: the ability to accurately describe or predict their own learned behaviors without explicit supervision. This capability raises safety concerns as it may, for example, allow models to better conceal their true abilities during evaluation. We attempt to characterize the minimal conditions under which such self-awareness emerges, and the mechanistic processes through which it manifests. Through controlled finetuning experiments on instruction-tuned LLMs with low-rank adapters (LoRA), we find: (1) that self-awareness can be reliably induced using a single rank-1 LoRA adapter; (2) that the learned self-aware behavior can be largely captured by a single steering vector in activation space, recovering nearly all of the fine-tune's behavioral effect; and (3) that self-awareness is non-universal and domain-localized, with independent representations across tasks. Together, these findings suggest that behavioral self-awareness emerges as a domain-specific, linear feature that can be easily induced and modulated.

papers.title: Latent Neural Representations Analysis and Distillation for Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we effectively distill Transformer models when there is a dimensionality mismatch between teacher and student, and how can analysis of latent neural representations (like outlier dimensions) inform better distillation algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces two novel distillation methods: Attention Map Alignment Distillation (AMAD) for handling mismatched attention heads between teacher and student models, and Emergent Outlier Focused Distillation (EOFD) which prioritizes critical outlier dimensions in latent representations. It also provides the first systematic analysis of emergent outlier dimensions in Encoder-Decoder T5 and instruction-finetuned Flan-T5 models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods for analyzing and distilling latent neural representations advance the understanding and acceleration of Transformer inference, with AMAD and EOFD demonstrating state-of-the-art distillation performance and generalization across architectures.
papers.key_findings:
AMAD enables effective distillation between teacher and student Transformers with different numbers of attention heads, outperforming conventional methods on vision-language tasks like VQA and captioning.
Outlier dimensions in T5 and Flan-T5 models, identified by unusually large activation magnitudes, are critical for zero-shot performance and are shared across layers within the encoder or decoder, but differ between encoder and decoder.
EOFD, which focuses distillation loss on these outlier dimensions, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GLUE benchmark and generalizes across BERT, GPT-2, and T5 architectures.
Distillation with AMAD can compensate for the absence of vision-language pre-training, and in some cases, distilled students outperform pre-trained and fine-tuned teachers.
The growth of outlier magnitude in T5 models is more correlated with increasing layer depth rather than overall model size, contrary to findings in GPT models.
papers.limitation: In some cases, a Teacher attention head may not be similar to any Student head after AMAD distillation, indicating a potential failure mode for knowledge transfer.
papers.abstract: Transformer-backed Large Language Models and Large Vision-Language Models are among the most widely used machine learning models recently. However, due to their enormous size, their behaviors and dynamics become difficult to understand and explain, and their inference speed and cost become slow and forbidding. Therefore, understanding their latent neural patterns and distilling their latent neural representations into smaller, cheaper, and faster models are vital for creating more explainable, accessible, and sustainable machine intelligence. However, knowledge distillation algorithms face an inherent challenge in minimizing the divergence between the neural activation representations of a teacher Transformer and a student Transformer: The latent representation spaces of the smaller Student always have lower dimensionality than those of the larger Teacher. We will address this Transformer distillation dimensionality mismatch or reduction problem by analyzing the neural activation patterns within these latent representation spaces and by proposing corresponding novel algorithms for distilling each group of components of Transformers. Our ultimate goal is to advance the field of understanding and accelerating the inference process of large Transformers by studying their latent neural representations.Specifically, we first develop novel algorithms for aligning the heads within the Multi-Head Attention components of these Transformers for latent neural representation distillation. We propose a new Attention Map Alignment Distillation (AMAD) method for Transformers with multi-head attention, which, unlike previous literature, can work for a Teacher and a Student with mismatched dimensionalities in terms of the numbers of attention heads. Specifically, we soft-align different heads in Teacher and Student attention maps using a cosine similarity weighting. The Teacher head contributes more to the Student heads for which it has a higher similarity weight. Each Teacher head contributes to all the Student heads by minimizing the divergence between the attention latent neural activation distributions for the soft-aligned heads.We then advance the understanding and distillation of the latent neural representations of the Feed Forward Network and Layer Normalization components of these Transformers. Previous literature shows that a small subset of dimensions within the high-dimensional latent neural representation spaces of language Transformers emerge as “outliers”, with weights or latent neuron activations of unusually large magnitudes—several standard deviations from the mean—during pretraining, and seem to encode critical linguistic knowledge in a sparse way. We systematically extend these previous findings on emergent outliers to Encoder-Decoder Transformers and instruction-finetuned models at scale, for the first time. We show that emergent outlier dimensions of the Transformer latent neural representations contribute significantly more to zero-shot performance than non-outlier dimensions. Leveraging our findings, we further propose the Emergent Outlier Focused Distillation (EOFD) method, which prioritizes these critical outlier latent dimensions to address the trade-off among these representation dimensions during distillation. Specifically, we propose a weighted MSE loss to place greater emphasis on the emergent outlier dimensions of the latent neural representations, which are identified by the standard deviations of neuron activation magnitudes.We demonstrate that our AMAD and EOFD distillation algorithms achieve state-of-the-art performance empirically and generalize well to different Transformer architectures. Specifically, for AMAD, we experiment on distilling VL-T5 and BLIP and apply the AMAD loss to their T5, BERT, and ViT sub-modules. We show that, under vision-language settings, AMAD outperforms conventional distillation methods on the VQA-2.0, COCO captioning, and Multi30K translation datasets. We further show that even without VL pre-training, the distilled VL-T5 models outperform corresponding VL pre-trained VL-T5 models that are further fine-tuned by ground-truth signals, and that fine-tuning distillation can also compensate to some degree for the absence of VL pre-training in BLIP models. As for EOFD, we empirically show that it outperforms state-of-the-art distillation methods on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark. We further demonstrate that EOFD generalizes well across Encoder-only BERT, Decoder-only GPT-2, and Encoder-Decoder T5 architectures.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Dissecting Fine-Tuning Unlearning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do fine-tuning-based unlearning methods appear successful in behavioral tests, and what is their actual mechanism and limitations?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods do not genuinely erase problematic knowledge; instead, they alter the model's knowledge retrieval process by modifying the coefficients in the MLP's final layers, which also negatively impacts unrelated knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods do not erase knowledge but alter knowledge extraction mechanisms, and they negatively impact the model's unrelated capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Restoring the value vectors in MLPs does not recover unlearned knowledge, indicating that the knowledge remains stored.
Restoring the attention states in intermediate and deeper layers recovers some knowledge, showing that attention components are involved in knowledge extraction.
Restoring the coefficients in the final layers of MLPs recovers most of the unlearned knowledge, indicating that these coefficients are the primary contributors to the unlearning effect.
Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods have a global negative effect, degrading the model's performance on unrelated knowledge.
The unlearning mechanism works by altering the model's knowledge retrieval process rather than erasing the knowledge itself.
papers.limitation: The experiments disregard potential unlearning impact from parameter changes in other model components (e.g., unembedding matrix and normalization layers), and it is unclear if these changes have meaningful effects.
future_direction: Future unlearning evaluations should focus on precise measurement of knowledge storage and retrieval dynamics.
Further investigation into defensive strategies based on the findings about MLP coefficients.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods prevail for preventing targeted harmful, sensitive, or copyrighted information within large language models while preserving overall capabilities. However, the true effectiveness of these methods is unclear. In this work, we delve into the limitations of fine-tuning-based unlearning through activation patching and parameter restoration experiments. Our findings reveal that these methods alter the model's knowledge retrieval process, providing further evidence that they do not genuinely erase the problematic knowledge embedded in the model parameters. Instead, the coefficients generated by the MLP components in the model's final layer are the primary contributors to these seemingly positive unlearning effects, playing a crucial role in controlling the model's behaviors. Furthermore, behavioral tests demonstrate that this unlearning mechanism inevitably impacts the global behavior of the models, affecting unrelated knowledge or capabilities. The code is released at https://github.com/yihuaihong/Dissecting-FT-Unlearning.

papers.title: REMIND: Input Loss Landscapes Reveal Residual Memorization in Post-Unlearning LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we detect residual memorization in unlearned LLMs using input loss landscapes, and does this approach outperform existing evaluation methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REMIND, a black-box evaluation method that uses input loss landscapes to detect residual memorization in unlearned LLMs, showing it outperforms existing methods and is robust across models and datasets.
papers.conclusion: REMIND provides a sensitive, practical, and black-box evaluation framework for detecting residual memorization in unlearned LLMs, offering a more reliable measure of unlearning effectiveness.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning reshapes the Input Loss Landscape (ILL), with forgotten data exhibiting flatter, less steep loss landscapes compared to retained or holdout data.
REMIND outperforms pointwise and other black-box baselines in detecting unlearning failures, demonstrating higher sensitivity and lower false-negative rates.
REMIND is robust across paraphrased inputs, different model architectures, benchmark datasets, and unlearning techniques.
ILL structure reveals intermediate forgetting signatures, indicating that forgetting is not binary but produces structured patterns in the loss landscape.
Embedding-proximity perturbation technique enables efficient and semantically grounded exploration of the local loss landscape without requiring model internals.
papers.limitation: Unlearning increases loss on forgotten samples but is bounded by the maximum loss observed on holdout data, indicating a potential tradeoff between effective forgetting and model generalization.
future_direction: Explore the tradeoff between forgetting and generalization in unlearning
Build upon the REMIND framework for further applications and monitoring unlearning progress during training
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a model without requiring full retraining. This capability is crucial for ensuring privacy, safety, and regulatory compliance. Therefore, verifying whether a model has truly forgotten target data is essential for maintaining reliability and trustworthiness. However, existing evaluation methods often assess forgetting at the level of individual inputs. This approach may overlook residual influence present in semantically similar examples. Such influence can compromise privacy and lead to indirect information leakage. We propose REMIND (Residual Memorization In Neighborhood Dynamics), a novel evaluation method aiming to detect the subtle remaining influence of unlearned data and classify whether the data has been effectively forgotten. REMIND analyzes the model's loss over small input variations and reveals patterns unnoticed by single-point evaluations. We show that unlearned data yield flatter, less steep loss landscapes, while retained or unrelated data exhibit sharper, more volatile patterns. REMIND requires only query-based access, outperforms existing methods under similar constraints, and demonstrates robustness across different models, datasets, and paraphrased inputs, making it practical for real-world deployment. By providing a more sensitive and interpretable measure of unlearning effectiveness, REMIND provides a reliable framework to assess unlearning in language models. As a result, REMIND offers a novel perspective on memorization and unlearning.

papers.title: Monitoring Latent World States in Language Models with Propositional Probes
papers.research_question: Can we extract a faithful latent world model (as logical propositions) from a language model's internal activations, and does this internal representation remain faithful even when the model's outputs are unfaithful?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces propositional probes, a method to extract symbolic latent world states (logical propositions) from LM activations, and shows these internal states remain faithful in adversarial settings where model outputs are unfaithful.
papers.conclusion: Evidence supports the hypotheses that LMs internally construct symbolic models of input contexts, and that these internal models can remain faithful even when the LM's outputs are influenced by unfaithful tendencies.
papers.key_findings:
Propositional probes can extract logical propositions from LM activations by compositionally combining domain probes using a binding similarity metric.
Probes generalize to complex inputs (short stories, Spanish) despite being trained only on simple templates.
In adversarial settings (prompt injection, backdoor attacks, gender bias), the decoded propositions remain faithful while the model's outputs are unfaithful.
A Hessian-based algorithm can identify a low-rank binding subspace that causally mediates binding between entities and attributes.
The binding similarity metric derived from this subspace enables accurate composition of propositions.
papers.limitation:
The binding similarity metric does not strongly distinguish between the second and third entity in a three-entity context, indicating the identified subspace may contain spurious, non-binding directions.
Propositional probes are partially susceptible to order information (e.g., in nested contexts), though they still capture semantic binding.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger worlds with more complex semantics by discovering representations of role-filler binding and state changes.
papers.abstract: Language models are susceptible to bias, sycophancy, backdoors, and other tendencies that lead to unfaithful responses to the input context. Interpreting internal states of language models could help monitor and correct unfaithful behavior. We hypothesize that language models represent their input contexts in a latent world model, and seek to extract this latent world state from the activations. We do so with 'propositional probes', which compositionally probe tokens for lexical information and bind them into logical propositions representing the world state. For example, given the input context ''Greg is a nurse. Laura is a physicist.'', we decode the propositions ''WorksAs(Greg, nurse)'' and ''WorksAs(Laura, physicist)'' from the model's activations. Key to this is identifying a 'binding subspace' in which bound tokens have high similarity (''Greg'' and ''nurse'') but unbound ones do not (''Greg'' and ''physicist''). We validate propositional probes in a closed-world setting with finitely many predicates and properties. Despite being trained on simple templated contexts, propositional probes generalize to contexts rewritten as short stories and translated to Spanish. Moreover, we find that in three settings where language models respond unfaithfully to the input context -- prompt injections, backdoor attacks, and gender bias -- the decoded propositions remain faithful. This suggests that language models often encode a faithful world model but decode it unfaithfully, which motivates the search for better interpretability tools for monitoring LMs.

papers.title: Discovering Undesired Rare Behaviors via Model Diff Amplification
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently detect rare, undesired behaviors in LLMs that emerge from post-training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces model diff amplification, a method to amplify differences between pre- and post-training logits to surface rare, undesired behaviors in LLMs, making them more detectable with fewer samples.
papers.conclusion: Model diff amplification is a practical tool for detecting rare, undesired behaviors in LLMs, though it overestimates prevalence and should be part of a larger evaluation pipeline.
papers.key_findings:
Amplification makes emergently misaligned responses 10 to 300 times more common, e.g., from 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 30 with 5% bad data.
For post-training monitoring, amplification detects harmful behaviors earlier, with compliance rising from 0 to 1 in 25 after only 5% of training.
In backdoor detection, amplification makes backdoored behavior 100 times more common, from 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 50.
The method is effective across different prompts and models, as shown in case studies.
Amplification produces coherent samples despite magnifying logit differences.
papers.limitation: The method is intended to surface uncommon behaviors and would overestimate their frequency, so it is not a way to measure prevalence.
future_direction: Developing better model organisms for sleeper agent research
Building out a comprehensive toolkit leveraging interpretability for evaluations and debugging
papers.abstract: How can we efficiently detect rare, undesired behaviors in LLMs that emerge from post-training? Introduces model diff amplification, a method to amplify differences between pre- and post-training logits to surface rare, undesired behaviors in LLMs, making them more detectable with fewer samples. Model diff amplification is a practical tool for detecting rare, undesired behaviors in LLMs, though it overestimates prevalence and should be part of a larger evaluation pipeline.

papers.title: On the Impact of Knowledge Distillation for Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does knowledge distillation improve model interpretability in addition to model accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Knowledge distillation improves model interpretability by transferring class-similarity information from teacher to student, making activation maps more object-centric.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge distillation enhances both the accuracy and interpretability of models, and this improvement is consistent across different KD methods, datasets, and notions of interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
KD increases the number of concept detectors (interpretability) compared to training from scratch.
KD improves interpretability by transferring class-similarity information, while label smoothing reduces interpretability.
The interpretability of student models improves as the amount of class-similarity information they learn increases.
Various KD methods (vanilla KD, AT, FT, CRD, SSKD, self-KD) all improve model interpretability.
KD improves interpretability across different datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR, MNIST, SST) and different interpretability measures (concept detectors, five-band-scores, DiffROAR, loss gradients).
future_direction: Determine whether KD can yield other useful results (e.g., model robustness).
Explore whether additional metrics can be used to measure model interpretability.
papers.abstract: Several recent studies have elucidated why knowledge distillation (KD) improves model performance. However, few have researched the other advantages of KD in addition to its improving model performance. In this study, we have attempted to show that KD enhances the interpretability as well as the accuracy of models. We measured the number of concept detectors identified in network dissection for a quantitative comparison of model interpretability. We attributed the improvement in interpretability to the class-similarity information transferred from the teacher to student models. First, we confirmed the transfer of class-similarity information from the teacher to student model via logit distillation. Then, we analyzed how class-similarity information affects model interpretability in terms of its presence or absence and degree of similarity information. We conducted various quantitative and qualitative experiments and examined the results on different datasets, different KD methods, and according to different measures of interpretability. Our research showed that KD models by large models could be used more reliably in various fields.

papers.title: Unmasking Backdoors: An Explainable Defense via Gradient-Attention Anomaly Scoring for Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: How can attention and gradient signals be combined to detect and neutralize backdoor triggers in pre-trained language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an explainable inference-time defense that combines attention and gradient signals to detect and neutralize backdoor triggers in pre-trained language models.
papers.conclusion: X-GRAAD is an effective and explainable defense against backdoor attacks in pre-trained language models, leveraging joint attribution signals for robust and transparent security.
papers.key_findings:
X-GRAAD significantly reduces attack success rates (ASR) across multiple models and datasets while maintaining clean accuracy.
The method provides interpretable insights through anomaly score distributions and trigger localization.
It generalizes effectively to different transformer architectures and attack types, including clean-label and multi-token triggers.
The defense is computationally efficient compared to retraining-based methods.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly when fine-tuned on large, domain-relevant datasets. However, they remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where adversaries embed malicious behaviors using trigger patterns in the training data. These triggers remain dormant during normal usage, but, when activated, can cause targeted misclassifications. In this work, we investigate the internal behavior of backdoored pre-trained encoder-based language models, focusing on the consistent shift in attention and gradient attribution when processing poisoned inputs; where the trigger token dominates both attention and gradient signals, overriding the surrounding context. We propose an inference-time defense that constructs anomaly scores by combining token-level attention and gradient information. Extensive experiments on text classification tasks across diverse backdoor attack scenarios demonstrate that our method significantly reduces attack success rates compared to existing baselines. Furthermore, we provide an interpretability-driven analysis of the scoring mechanism, shedding light on trigger localization and the robustness of the proposed defense.

papers.title: Reviving Your MNEME: Predicting The Side Effects of LLM Unlearning and Fine-Tuning via Sparse Model Diffing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically detect unintended side effects in fine-tuned or unlearned large language models without access to fine-tuning data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MNEME, a framework that uses sparse model diffing to detect unintended side effects in fine-tuned or unlearned LLMs without access to fine-tuning data, achieving high accuracy across multiple scenarios.
papers.conclusion: MNEME is a general-purpose framework that effectively detects side effects in fine-tuned or unlearned LLMs using sparse model diffing, highlighting the promise of scalable, data-agnostic auditing tools.
papers.key_findings:
MNEME achieves up to 95% accuracy in predicting side effects on WMDP unlearning tasks.
On emergent misalignment, MNEME achieves 68.2% accuracy with perfect precision.
In benign fine-tuning scenarios, MNEME shows strong performance with up to 92.9% accuracy.
Sparse model diffing effectively isolates behavioral shifts without requiring fine-tuning data.
Retraining on high-activation samples can partially reverse the detected side effects.
papers.limitation:
Relies on task-agnostic corpora which may not reflect specific fine-tuning distributions.
Interpretability pipeline depends on LLM-generated descriptions, which may introduce noise or imprecision.
Cross-Coder was not originally designed for model diffing, and architectural constraints may limit fine-grained change capture.
Provides correlational insights rather than causal guarantees.
Computationally demanding due to need for model activations and large-scale inference.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are frequently fine-tuned or unlearned to adapt to new tasks or eliminate undesirable behaviors. While existing evaluation methods assess performance after such interventions, there remains no general approach for detecting unintended side effects, such as unlearning biology content degrading performance on chemistry tasks, particularly when these effects are unpredictable or emergent.
